message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 on consumer devices). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores. |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, branch prediction, large caches, and sophisticated control logic. | Simpler, lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work individually but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich instruction sets (x86, ARM) with support for complex operations, branching, and varied data types. | Often a reduced instruction set tailored for SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, fast access to main memory. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies heavily on high‑bandwidth shared memory (VRAM). |
| **Workload pattern** | Serial or lightly parallel tasks where latency matters more than raw throughput. | Highly parallel tasks where the same operation is performed on many data elements at once (e.g., matrix multiplication, image filtering). |
| **Typical use cases** | Running operating systems, web browsers, office software, general programming. | Rendering 3D graphics, video encoding/decoding, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training. |
| **Power efficiency** | Optimized for low power consumption per core on mobile CPUs; higher power on desktop CPUs due to performance focus. | Designed for high throughput per watt; GPUs consume a lot of power when fully utilized. |

In short, a CPU excels at handling diverse, sequential tasks quickly, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation on many pieces of data simultaneously. That’s why modern applications often offload heavy numeric or image‑processing work to the GPU even though it’s not strictly a “graphics” device anymore.
